title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
abstract: This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system). For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook. Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale. Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs. New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline. Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motiva

title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary
abstract: This latest deep dive into Meta’s Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) takes a look at PrivacyLib. A privacy requirement must hold as data moves through Meta’s diverse data and processing systems. Historically, supporting a new requirement meant implementing the same enforcement logic separately in each system. PrivacyLib replaces this with a common library that runs inside the clients of Meta’s data and processing systems. A system integrates with PrivacyLib once, and new privacy capabilities plug in as modules that reuse that integration. PrivacyLib performs billions of checks every second, and changes are simulated and rolled out per module. For internal AI agents, whose data access paths may not be known in advance, tool calls on supported paths carry agent context to PrivacyLib. The propagated context links each access to its session, so modules can observe data use and block operations that are not allowed. At Meta, many privacy requirements ultimately come down to the same question: Can we prove that a piece of data goes only where it is allowed? At Meta’s scale, rather than relying solely on manual privacy audits, which can go out of sync as systems change, we have developed Privacy Aware Infrastructure (PAI) to answer this question within the infrastructure itself. PAI offers efficient and reliable first-class privacy constructs embedded in Meta’s infrastructure so that products can keep evolving quickly. In previous posts, we have covered how data understanding , data lineage , and Policy Zones (our information flow control technology) play a role in PAI. Now, we are diving deep into PrivacyLib , a common library that runs inside the clients of hundreds of our data and processing systems at the point of data access. PrivacyLib plays an important role in the final stage of the broader PAI workflow: continuously enforcing and monitoring data flows. This blog post focuses on PrivacyLib’s role in the final stage of the PAI workflow. Before PrivacyLib, we integrated privacy enforcement separately into the clients of each data and processing system for each requirement. With this approach, implementing a new requirement across systems could take months. Each new requirement, whether purpose limitation or data flow discovery, needed the same set of capabilities: covering a wide range of systems; deploying in weeks rather than months; running on every data access without becoming a latency problem; and rolling out enforcement changes without taking the fleet down. Over time, this approach became harder to scale as requirements and systems evolved. PrivacyLib separates system integration from requirement implementation. We integrate each system once. When a requirement can be met at the point of data access, we implement it as a PrivacyLib module shared across the systems already integrated, so a new requirement no longer needs a separate implementation in each system. There are two kinds of modules: Enforcing modules can block a data access. For example, Policy Zones enforces purpose limitation . Observing modules only record a data access. For example, Privacy Probes collects the runtime signals used to discover data flows. As internal AI agents became a new way of accessing data, we also added the Agent Observability module to observe agent-related data access events and help safeguard the data that agents can reach. Systems already integrated with PrivacyLib picked it up without new integration work, which is what integrating once buys: each new privacy capability arrives as a module, not as a project. PrivacyLib replaces repeated implementations across systems. Engineering Challenges and Approaches of PrivacyLib at Meta’s Scale PrivacyLib operates across a broad range of data access paths at Meta: More than a hundred libraries used to access data services, from key/value stores to AI features. Thousands of production services with versions of the deployed library. Millions of assets being accessed daily. Billions of checks

title: Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape
abstract: The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty. For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next. Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty. Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities: Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks. Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them. Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work , especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward. AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs. AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options. Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else. Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors: “I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.” “Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.” When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help. The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows . Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does. Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. title: Meta Networking at the 2026 OCP Global Summit: Open Innovation for Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across AI Networks
abstract: At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark , and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster . Highlights IcePack & IceCube: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack with 102.4T switch blades (128×800G, Broadcom Tomahawk 6C and NVIDIA Spectrum-6 variants), running FBOSS. Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) for scale-out: Meta’s multi-plane scale-out fabric where each GPU connects to eight network planes. 3-tier → 2-tier Clos, NIC-level packet spraying, and a combined host+switch control plane. Built with NVIDIA and shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across: BAG, our petabit-scale super-spine joining buildings, campuses, and regions in our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster , plus SRv6 regional backbones on FBOSS + SAI. Ethernet for scale-up : Tahan, the Ethernet scale-up switch for MTIA 300 based on Broadcom Tomahawk5; a preview of 72 accelerators per rack on 102.4T silicon; and ESUN progressing from 1.0 → 1.1. OSPA: a new OCP initiative co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba to standardize the switch platform layer . v1.0 spec submitted to OCP. MetaRoCE: our RDMA transport for AI networks , now going open source. We shared insights into key networking-related initiatives through talks from many of the Meta network and hardware teams. Those talks and their slide decks are now available to everyone! Keynote and Executive Sessions Concrete to Code: Engineering AI Infrastructure at Gigawatt Scale ( video ) AI has changed the shape of infrastructure. Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure at Meta, shares how Meta is designing, building, and operating at a scale that requires rethinking the network, the facility, and the systems that hold it all together. Speaker: Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure, Meta Betting on the Network: Meta’s Case for Full-Stack, Open AI Networking ( video ) AI progress now depends on the network as much as on compute. The path forward is a full-stack, open approach built in the open ecosystem rather than behind proprietary walls. Speaker: Omar Baldonado, Senior Director, Data Center & AI Networking, Meta Breaking the Walls: Open Scale-Across for the AI Era ( video ) Training compute is compounding faster than infrastructure can scale. This talk lays out why open scale-across networking is needed to connect AI capacity across data centers and regions. Speakers: Vipul Deokar, VP, Core Network Infrastructure, Meta; Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon & Systems Architecture and Engineering Fellow, Cisco; Tom Williams, VP, Marketing, Cisco Switch Platforms, Optics, and Interconnect Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch ( video ) IceCube is Meta’s 102.4T switch that goes into our liquid-cooled Icepack rack. Icecube and N-IceCube are based on a 2OU, hybrid liquid/air-cooled, PHY-less design and incorporate either the Broadcom Tomahawk 6C or NVIDIA Spectrum-6 ASICs with 128x800GE of non-blocking capacity. Speakers: Rongchun Zhou, Network Hardware Engineer, Meta; Reza Niazmand, Network Technical Program Manager, Meta Integrated Optics at Scale: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta’s 102.4T ( video ) A look at why integrated optics matter for rack-scale AI — power, density, disaggregation, and reliability — and what Meta learned validating 51.2T co-packaged optics that could carry over to 102.4T. title: Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: If you’ve tried to get an agent into production, the model and tool use are not the blocker. The main bottleneck is everything around them: how many teams can build within a secure environment, which team owns each model and tool, how AgentOps and error handling stay inside a pre-defined boundary, and how platform, Workstream, and finance teams see cost and health across accounts. For a Platform team that wants to support many agentic use cases, that’s a platform product to design and operate. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Workstream teams. Workstream teams are the domain or product teams that build and own agents on the platform. Each Workstream team needs a paved road with approved models and tools, short-lived workload identity, isolated runtime and memory, automated evaluation, rollback, telemetry, and cost attribution. These controls need to remain consistent as Workstream teams customize prompts, tools, data access, and application behavior. When every team assembles them, controls drift, shared services become a bottleneck, and ownership is difficult to audit. In this post, we walk through the architecture and reference implementation of an enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover the multi-account operating model, the Platform control plane, a repeatable per-Workstream deployment pattern, separate inference and tool gateways, and an evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before promotion to production. By the end, you should be able to deploy a governed Workstream from the companion blueprint, validate its security and lifecycle contracts, and use it as the foundation for your own agentic AI platform in the organization. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides modular services for building, deploying, and operating agents at scale, including runtime, gateway, identity, memory, policy, registry, and evaluations. The Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint , built on AgentCore, adds the surrounding enterprise contracts as deployable infrastructure as code: ownership, account boundaries, software delivery, observability, cost governance, and retirement. Architectural principles Before diving into the solution details, it helps to understand the organizational needs that drive the platform architecture. The common challenges we have heard from customers who establish an agent platform fall into these five categories: Governed model access: Every untrusted inference request must pass through an approved inference gateway. The gateway applies the organization’s guardrails (for example, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails or a third-party provider), restricts which models and inference AWS Regions each Workstream can use, and enforces per-Workstream rate limits, token quotas, and budgets so that no single team can exhaust shared capacity. It also carries workload identity and emits attribution data. Governed tool access: Agents must discover and invoke only approved tools through an authenticated Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, with exact targets, least-privilege execution roles, policy decisions, and an auditable owner. Delegated delivery: Workstream teams (for example, product teams) need to ship and roll back independently inside pre-approved boundaries, without waiting for the platform team to deploy each application or granting developers a direct infrastructure write path. Fleet operations and cost: Several personas need visibility across accounts without gaining write access to team workloads. Agent operations engineers need logs, metrics, traces, and quotas. Workstream owners need cost per agent against their budgets. FinOps and finance teams need chargeback by team or business unit through AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) . Security and governance leads need evidence of which workload called which model and tool. Bounded evidence and lifecycle: Every agent release

title: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS
abstract: What usually stops PyTorch training from scaling out to a cluster is the container, not the model code. Every container needs the same CUDA runtime , a PyTorch build compiled against it, NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library), the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) userspace libraries, the AWS OFI NCCL plugin that connects NCCL to EFA, and a Ray version the cluster operator agrees with. Building that image and rebuilding it each time one of those pieces moves is a project of its own, and it has nothing to do with the model you set out to train. The Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC) is that image, built by AWS. AWS assembles the stack, tests it as one unit, publishes it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public and keeps it patched. Figure 1: One EKS cluster with a control plane managed by AWS, a CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) running the KubeRay operator and Ray head, and two EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge nodes in one Availability Zone. KubeRay builds it from one RayCluster manifest, Ray Train places eight workers, one per GPU, and inter-node collectives cross over EFA. Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two roles. The Ray head coordinates and runs the global control store that tracks cluster state, the dashboard and job server you submit jobs to. Ray worker nodes supply the GPUs and run the training processes. Each worker joins the cluster by connecting to the head’s address when it starts. On Kubernetes, each of these is a pod. Kubernetes has no built-in idea of a Ray cluster, so something must create the head and worker pods, start Ray in the right role in each, point the workers at the head, and replace pods that fail. KubeRay does this. It’s an open source Kubernetes operator that adds a RayCluster resource: you describe a head group and a worker group in one manifest, and KubeRay builds and maintains the cluster from it. A single tagged image runs as both the Ray head and the Ray workers, whether KubeRay starts it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or you start it yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). What you add is configuration: which instances, how many GPUs each pod gets, which network transport NCCL uses, and which extra Python packages a job needs. All of it is set from outside the image. This post walks through a sample that uses the DLC exactly as published to fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances. The training code is one function, the cluster is one RayCluster manifest plus a file of variables, and no image is built at any point. Because the DLC already carries the EFA stack, collectives between the two instances run over the EFA as soon as the pods request it. The entire solution is in this sample repository , and it uses the same KubeRay-on-EKS foundation as our multi-node Ray Serve walkthrough . What you get without building anything The Ray Train DLC is the PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries on top. title: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3
abstract: As quality assurance (QA) automation adoption grows inside an organization, a new problem appears that has nothing to do with writing tests. A platform team stands up test automation, then a second team wants to join, then a dozen more. Soon hundreds of test cases belong to different products and squads, and everyone can see everyone else’s tests. No one can answer a basic question at a glance: is this application’s test coverage healthy right now? Test authoring stops being the bottleneck. Organizing tests and controlling who can touch them becomes the work. A second, related question follows close behind: who owns this application and its tests, and who is accountable when coverage slips? Without a clear owner, health problems have no one to land on. In the first post , we introduced QA Studio, a reference solution built with Amazon Nova Act . Teams use it to define tests in natural language and run them through AI-powered visual navigation. In the second post , we added test suites and a CLI for batch regression testing in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. In this post, we cover two capabilities that help QA Studio scale across an organization. The first, applications , organizes tests and reports health metrics. The second, team-based user management , controls who can see and change what. Organizing tests with applications An application in QA Studio represents the system under test: a website, a web app, a service front end. It’s the container that gives a collection of tests, a home, and an owner. Use cases (the individual tests from Part 1) and test suites (the regression collections from Part 2) belong to an application, and they inherit its ownership. Instead of one flat list of every test in the deployment, each team works inside the applications they own. Creating an application takes a name, a base URL, and an optional set of environments such as development, staging, and production. From the application page, teams create new use cases directly in context, add existing ones, and group them into test suites. This is also where QA Studio reports on the health of the tests it runs. Figure 1: The application detail page, showing pass rate, executions, and failures with the use cases and test suites tabs Understanding application health with metrics Tests produce results. Understanding those results over time is what tells a team whether the development lifecycle for an application is healthy, not only whether a single build is ready for release. QA Studio records the outcome of every execution as Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics, dimensioned by application and by environment. It turns these metrics into a health view on the application page. The top of the page answers the immediate question with three figures: the pass rate over the selected window, the total number of executions, and the current failure count. Alongside them, QA Studio computes a health score of 0–100. The score starts from the pass rate and subtracts a penalty for flaky tests. That way, an application whose tests pass but flip between pass and fail doesn’t present a falsely perfect picture. A team scanning a portfolio of applications can tell the stable ones from the ones that need attention without opening each result. The metrics tab moves from the current snapshot to trends. Teams choose a 7-day window with hourly granularity or a 30-day window with daily granularity, and QA Studio charts executions, successes, failures, and average duration across that period. Because the underlying metrics carry an environment dimension, teams filter the view to a single environment. For example, they can compare how staging behaves against production for the same set of tests. Two views target the tests that cost teams the most time. title: AWS named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service
abstract: I’m proud to share that Amazon Web Services (AWS) has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS) for Amazon Connect for the fourth consecutive year. We believe this recognition reflects years of work pushing on what’s possible in customer experience. When we launched Amazon Connect Customer, we set out to evolve how businesses serve their customers: to make personalized, intelligent experiences possible without giving up efficiency, flexibility, or control. That belief still drives how we build today. Customer expectations have shifted. People expect you to recognize them, understand what they need, and stay consistent across every channel. They don’t want to repeat themselves. They don’t want to navigate disconnected systems to solve a simple problem. They want interactions that feel natural, relevant, and genuinely helpful. Meeting that takes more than traditional contact center technology, it takes a comprehensive solution that brings together customer context, AI, and the flexibility to adapt. That’s what we’re building with Amazon Connect Customer. Customer experience without compromise What matters most to your customers hasn’t changed: they want to be known, they want their problems fully resolved, and they want to trust you in the moments that matter. Read the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant to know why we are recognized. Experiences that start with knowing the customer. Connect Customer builds a living picture of every customer: who they are, what they’ve been through, what they need next. Every touchpoint draws on that intelligence. Your customer feels known before a single word is exchanged. That’s what personal actually looks like. Resolution that carries all the way through. Most of the industry is still optimizing for deflection: getting customers away from humans as fast as possible. We took a different path. Connect Customer is built for the hard things: the disputed claim, the renegotiated mortgage, the disrupted itinerary that needs real action and can’t go wrong. We carry those interactions all the way through to resolution, and we make them feel natural and personal. Generative and agentic AI push this further: understanding what a customer needs and acting on it. Every action is auditable. Humans step in when the moment calls for it. You get enterprise scale and the confidence that nothing slips through the cracks. Building for what’s next The companies that win the next decade of customer experience won’t be the ones with the most channels or the fastest bot. They’ll be the ones whose customers feel known, whose problems actually get resolved, and whose trust is earned in the moments that matter most. Connect Customer exists to make that real for businesses of every size. I’m proud of the Connect Customer team for receiving this recognition for the fourth year in a row. Our engineers, product teams, partners, and customers shaped what we’ve built. This is a moment to celebrate how far we’ve come, and a signal of what’s ahead. Every customer is unique. Every interaction should reflect that. title: Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs
abstract: Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits. Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress. For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job. Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs , which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job. With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy-loads your container image. It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes. You adopt it by pointing to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image. Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels. The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure. SOCI-indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance. As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks. This post shows how to adopt SOCI indexing: what it is, the results we measured, and how to turn it on for your own jobs. The challenge SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance. It decompresses and writes every layer to disk. For small images this takes seconds. But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more. That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time. The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime. How SOCI indexing works Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images. Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately. It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it. A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image. You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI-compliant artifact linked to your original image. Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid. SageMaker AI checks for an index automatically When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly: Scenario What happens The image includes a SOCI index SageMaker AI lazy-loads the image and starts your container before the full download completes The image has no SOCI index Standard download, no change in behavior The index can’t be read, or lazy loading doesn’t succeed The job falls back to a standard download and continues running Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running. You only gain faster startup. You never risk breaking an existing workflow. What we measured We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI-indexed lazy loading. We then ran full training jobs from both to measure the effect on training speed. Setup Eight images , 1.8–35.4 GB compressed. title: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: This post was co-authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder. The engineering team at Property Finder , a digital real estate application, discovered that 96.8 percent of their evaluation labels had been inherited directly from a single model’s predictions rather than verified by human experts. Their ground truth was systematically skewed toward the incumbent model, making every alternative appear to underperform. The labels also had errors, but the bias was what blocked objective model comparison. They uncovered this when migrating their vision AI workload to a more cost-effective option on Amazon Bedrock . Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images every day across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Their system evaluates 11 quality attributes per image. These cover watermark detection, room classification, furnishing status, photo quality, and construction indicators. That’s thousands of new property listings with an average of 15 images each. All need quality assessment before going live. Property Finder needed a more cost-effective option. But measured against those labels, any alternative was at a disadvantage. The hardest part was not finding a better model. It was discovering that their evaluation methodology itself was the blocker. In this post, we share how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to select the right model on Amazon Bedrock, achieving higher accuracy at 86 percent lower cost. We walk through the methodology and iteration examples, with lessons you can apply to your own workloads. The following figure illustrates the prompt optimization loop that Property Finder and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team used to iteratively improve classification accuracy on Amazon Bedrock. Figure 1: Prompt optimization loop architecture The diagram shows the iterative prompt optimization cycle. A property image is processed by Amazon Bedrock, which outputs the predicted attributes in JSON format. During optimization, these predictions are scored with Micro F1 against the 256-image expert-annotated development set. Error analysis then inspects failed images and identifies visual patterns, which inform the next prompt version. The loop ran from v0 to v27. AI assistants helped refine the prompts, and later versions used automated optimization. Your evaluation might be lying Many teams encounter this scenario. You want to compare vision models, so you build an evaluation dataset. The most common way to get labels is to run your current model and treat its outputs as ground truth. The model has been running in production and nobody complained, so the labels must be good enough. But this creates a circular evaluation where any alternative gets judged by how closely it matches the incumbent’s behavior, not by actual correctness. Property Finder’s evaluation dataset had exactly this problem. Of their labeled samples, 96.8 percent came directly from the predictions of the existing vision language model (VLM) rather than independent human verification. Any alternative model was structurally disadvantaged before a single image was even processed. Hidden errors confirmed the severity. Watermark text extraction had character-level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters. Photo classification forced single labels onto images containing multiple room types. In the remaining 3.2 percent of human-labeled samples, annotators had introduced categories outside the original specification, like Office appearing where no such label existed in the prompt. A model comparison loses validity when the answer key was written by the model you are trying to replace. Building ground truth you can trust To break the cycle, you need human experts with real domain knowledge doing fresh annotations independently. No reference to previous model outputs. No a

title: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization
abstract: Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems that deliver reliable power for energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers. Its flagship product, the Exowatt P3, captures solar energy through optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long-duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand through a heat engine. Unlike grid-tied photovoltaic solar systems, P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, helping data centers come online without waiting in multi-year grid interconnection queues. Exowatt builds a fleet of AI agents that monitor and triage live alarms and support operational decisions for solar systems, often at the edge, with limited or no connectivity. As its fleet scales from test benches toward manufacturing and thousands of deployed field units, the intelligence layer that operates these systems must scale with it. In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline. The pipeline produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost. The two models described here are the first outputs of that pipeline rather than the end goal. The more durable result of the engagement was the pipeline itself: a repeatable path from raw operational data to a certified training set, a fine-tuned model, and an evaluated deployment artifact. Exowatt can now run this path in days rather than months. Alarm triage and energy-market analysis are two of many narrow, high-value tasks where the same approach applies. The challenge: AI on physical energy infrastructure Exowatt’s energy management system (EMS) runs across a growing fleet of operational sites. Each site continuously produces alarms: a hardware component operating out of spec, a dropped connection, an out-of-range voltage reading, and similar events. As the fleet scales toward thousands of field units, a human operator can’t monitor every site in real time. Exowatt needed an AI agent that could read the alarm state on each site and take or recommend the correct next action autonomously and reliably. A frontier model couldn’t solve this problem for three reasons: The task is narrow and proprietary. Alarm triage on Exowatt’s EMS depends on their specific hardware, data, and operating logic. A general-purpose frontier model isn’t specialized for it. It must run at the edge, with no GPU and often no internet. Many sites have limited or intermittent connectivity, so an agent that depends on a cloud call to a frontier model leaves the operator without coverage when the connection drops. Cost doesn’t scale at fleet level. Routing every operational decision to a frontier model across thousands of sites is not economical for a decision that repeats continuously. This is where Exowatt turned to model customization. Exowatt’s initial fine-tuning workflow relied on selecting an open-weight model, building a container, and creating a custom training recipe before any experiment could run. This was a major blocker for model experimentation. Additionally, they had to decide GPU hardware requirements of model fine-tuning. As the team increased the pace of experimentation, each run first required choosing a specific GPU instance type and then waiting for that self-selected capacity to become available. When a chosen instance type was unavailable, this could delay the start of a run or block it entirely. They needed a model small enough to run on a no-GPU edge controller, yet accurate enough compared to the frontier model on the specific task to act autonomously. Fine-tuning closed that gap: a compact, task-specialized model that is both deployable in the cloud and at the edge. Solution overview Exowatt addressed these challenges by adopting a cloud-native, serverless model customization approach on Amazon SageMaker AI. The same training pipeline produces fine-tuned models for two deployment targe

title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
abstract: Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one. This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute. The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository . Solution overview The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices. Figure 1: Solution architecture The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history. The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved. The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. Both are ready for whatever delivery mechanism your plant uses. Prerequisites To deploy the sampl

title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again. In the movie Groundhog Day , Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years. Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again. Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price. In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent. What an agent sends to its LLM Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains: Tool list – The definitions of every function the agent can call. Changes when you ship a new release. Instructions – The developer prompt: rules, persona, policies, examples. Also changes per release. History – Everything that happened in this session so far: the task, the model’s tool calls, and the tool results (which grows every turn). New turn – The latest tool result or user message (which might be different every time). What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching: Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn How prompt caching works under the hood When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill . During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token. Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint . You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so. Turn 1 compared to turn 2 Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both? For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically. New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents. Hello cached

title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
abstract: This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated. It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question , and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen. Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works. In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published. Amazon Bedrock now offers a managed knowledge base (Type: MANAGED), which owns the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval itself. The OpenSearch Serverless collection and index that post provisions are no longer something you need to create, scale, or pay for with OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the agentic half , a Gateway that exposes each knowledge base as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool, a Runtime that hosts the reasoning agent, and AgenticRetrieveStream, which reranks internally and returns a synthesized, cited answer. Agentic retrieval is available only on the Managed Knowledge Base. The observability and evaluation story is now something you can provision , not something you bolt on. This solution ships two Amazon CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation, on-demand and continuous, from the same deployment. This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order. If you read the 2024 post , the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
abstract: By Praneeth Yenugutala , Victor Dusa , Anastasia Samoilova , Megan Ren , Justin Wei , Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive , an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro . It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic. Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked. To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes. Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim). Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates. The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough. title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
abstract: Serdar Cellat , Yuchen Xie , Bernadette Marcu , Blaid Burgess , Cody Jarrett , Carlos Pereira , Qing Shi , Samuel Carvajal , Manuel Pamplona , Dorothy Jung , Feiko Ritsema , Benjamin Klein , Alex Woo , Eugene Lok , Anna Pulido , Rebecka Swe , Sanford Holsapple , Ranjith Kumar Shetty Introduction Clips in the Netflix mobile app. At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips , our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort. Our Video Resizing Approach Converting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot. We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead. An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios. Shot Detection and Splitting First, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles. Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop. Focus Region Discovery Once shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera. Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing. Temporal Reframing Once we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic. The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path. The PHP Incident
abstract: The PHP security incident is now (almost) old news. The timeline looks something like this : In late August, Wiz Research discovered two serious remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP called PHP2Shell. They reported the vulnerabilities to the PHP team on August 24, which started working on fixes on September 21. Amazon apparently detected PHP2Shell in the wild on October 17 (four days prior to disclosure). On October 20, details of the two vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were leaked prematurely. The next day, October 21, the PHP team released patches. If that were the end of the story, it wouldn’t be notable. But the problem goes a lot deeper. Although PHP is no longer fashionable, it runs a huge portion of the public internet. WordPress, Drupal, and Wikimedia run on top of PHP, and people who build on top of these tools are understandably not interested in chasing the latest hot technology. “ Choose Boring Technology ” is one of my favorite technical essays, and PHP is nothing if not boring. It’s well known and understood, and replacing something so widely used subjects you to a steep learning curve and new bugs and vulnerabilities. One problem is that PHP has a long history. According to Wiz, the vulnerabilities are present in versions going back to PHP 5.4. The PHP Foundation has released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and said that all instances of PHP need to be updated to one of those releases. Sites that can’t be updated should be taken offline and isolated. Upgrading an ancient PHP installation is a task that’s likely to fall on organizations least capable of undertaking it. There are plenty of ancient WordPress installations that haven’t been updated in years. There were so many fires to put out, and PHP pretty much “just worked”; running an old version wasn’t causing problems, and with so much else to do, why ask for trouble? Unfortunately, choosing boring technology doesn’t mean ignoring updates. And those who decided not to ask for trouble are now in plenty of trouble. This situation demonstrates the power of the latest foundation models to uncover vulnerabilities. Wiz used Wiz Atlas (its own model), Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to discover the vulnerability, which isn’t a single bug but a combination of several bugs that have been present for years but were obscure enough and apparently harmless enough to escape detection or repair. As Wiz says, The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. That’s the new frontier in security: finding ways to exploit chains of minor, unfixed, and sometimes undiscovered bugs in novel ways. Wiz was working responsibly with the PHP team to repair the vulnerability. The implications of this, however, are far broader than the fix to PHP, or even the thousands of PHP sites that need upgrades and are now vulnerable to attack. This incident shows dramatically how the gap between the discovery of a vulnerability and its exploitation has dropped. Since exploitation began before the RCEs were prematurely leaked, it makes sense to assume that some other organization had access to models capable of discovering the vulnerability. Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol are publicly available, though with guardrails that limit their usefulness for security research. I’m willing to assume that Wiz had access to the unrestricted version, but I doubt that the PHP team did. There are certainly other models, including open-weight models, that could be used to find vulnerabilities. Regardless of your stance on restricting model capabilities (I think those limitations are more damaging than helpful), it’s clear that Pandora’s box has been opened. No amount of wishful thinking will undo that. It’s also clear that we—an

title: Are You Getting Your Money’s Worth From AI?
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Software development has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of AI automation. One CIO I talked to recently, with 170 people in his organization, measured a 2.1x increase in productivity from AI. That productivity came at a cost. His top users of AI each spent $21,000 on tokens per month. Another engineering leader spends six to eight thousand dollars per engineer per month. This is not a trivial amount of money. Eventually, it has to come from somewhere, and it will probably come from your personnel budget. Now we’re talking about real consequences for real people’s lives. But there are also real business consequences for not acting. If you’re going to make those choices—and somebody is going to—they need to be good ones. So you need to know more than the costs; you need to know the benefits too. Are you getting a good return on your investment in AI? Is there another way of using AI that would be better? How do you know what you’re getting? Anecdotal reports abound, but the reasoning behind those anecdotes are often, to put it politely, not ideal. Some claims are outright fiction. Given the stakes, that’s a problem. In this essay series, I’ll show you how to assess the impact of AI on software development in your organization. It’s in four parts plus an epilogue: Why, and what not to do (this essay) Measuring delivery speed Measuring and modeling unintended consequences Modeling and forecasting business outcomes Epilogue: Notes for your CFO Why you need to quantify impact Engineering leaders everywhere are feeling pressure to do more with AI. But which approach is best? There are a lot of people with strident opinions about what to do, but not a lot of consensus, and even less hard data. Even if there were hard data, it’s not one-size-fits-all. A solution that works best for an internal IT development shop isn’t necessarily the one that works best for a startup, and the approach that’s best for a new product isn’t necessarily the one that’s best for a crafty legacy system. Faster approaches aren’t necessarily better, either. If you get twice as much done per person, but spend so much money on tokens that you have to cut your staff in half, have you actually seen any ROI? You might actually be better off with a more modest speed boost if it keeps your costs down. You can’t make these trade-offs from a gut feeling alone. In a famous METR study , engineers thought AI made them 49% faster than it actually did. 1 You have to measure impact to know what you’re actually getting. Don’t neglect costs Costs are much easier to measure than impact, but they’re not without their own challenges. The biggest one is subsidies. In the fight to gain market share, big AI firms are offering substantial discounts. One engineering leader told me each team member was spending thousands of dollars in tokens at the cost of a $200 subscription. Anthropic and OpenAI are constantly offering discounts and other promotions. At some point, these subsidies will end, and prices will go up. Or will they? Open-weight models and local inference are exerting downward pressure on token costs. Dedicated inference chips could make tokens cheaper. Routers promise to direct your prompts to the cheapest model for the job. Models could require fewer tokens to accomplish the same task as they become more capable. All of these factors could actually cause prices to go down. When you calculate ROI, don’t assume today’s costs are the ones you should model. Whether you think prices will go up, down, or remain the same, make your assumptions explicit, and consider modeling both optimistic and pessimistic scenarios. One more wrinkle: Adopting AI isn’t a matter of flipping a switch. People will need time to learn how to apply it. As with any big shift, change management isn’t to be underestimated. title: Are agent harnesses dying? What harness distillation changes.
abstract: The following article originally appeared on The Arize Blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Every time you think you’ve just got the hang of this AI thing, another thing gets declared “dead.” This week, it’s agent harnesses . Back in ancient history, aka June, I wrote a piece called “ Frameworks are dying, harnesses are winning ” and I don’t take that back. But this week a research team took a specialized agent harness, trained its behavior into a model and then took the harness away. The trained model handily beat the original model+harness combination. So are harnesses done now? Betteridge’s Law applies, so the answer is “no.” But the job of the agent harness is changing. Parts of a harness that are sufficiently generalizable can be trained into the model. That leaves your harness holding the things that make your application unique: your tools, your data, your users, and your environment. You still have to build a harness , but you have to be prepared to regularly throw it away and rebuild it to keep up with evolving models. This blog is about why that’s true, and how to turn “constantly rebuilding your harness” into an automatic process, not a giant time suck. How Harness-Zero trained an agent harness into a model First, the paper that kicked off this train of thought for me: it’s called “ Harness-Zero ,” from Haoran Ye and colleagues at Peking University. Its subject is harness distillation, i.e., training a model to reproduce behavior that used to be the result of the harness. The methodology is a little involved, so stick with me. First, the team built a specialized harness for a small model, Qwen3.5-9B. An automated loop, run with Kimi K3, analyzed where the small model kept failing on training tasks and added the usual components to fix those failures: custom tools, middleware rules that block risky actions, skills files and memory. They called this the “evolved harness.” Then they used that harness to generate training data. They put the small model through training tasks inside a minimal harness while a stronger model, GPT-5.6 Sol, reviewed every step the small model proposed. Sol used a copy of the evolved harness to tell it whether that step was a good idea. Sol passed good ideas from the small model through unchanged, and whenever the small model and the guidance disagreed, Sol made the smallest fix needed before the step ran. That gave them a bunch of training runs and, crucially, data about what needed to be corrected. Then they created the distilled model: They fine-tuned the small model on the corrected runs. Then they removed the evolved harness, the reviewer, and everything else. They then tested both the evolved harness and the distilled model head-to-head on spreadsheet editing, multi-app tool use, and chemistry. The distilled model’s average task success rose 21 points versus its untrained predecessor. That’s more than the untrained model gained with the full evolved harness attached. So the distilled model wasn’t just as good as the model+harness, it was noticeably better. What harness distillation can and cannot move into the model It’s not that the distilled model ran with no harness whatsoever: It still ran inside a minimal loop with one Bash tool, and the authors say that their method narrows what a harness has to provide rather than eliminating it entirely. The distilled model also didn’t win every competition: In chemistry, where the task is predicting which molecules combine to make a target compound, the distilled model trailed the harnessed version by eight points. The harness there supplied chemistry knowledge, candidate-generation logic, and a molecule validation tool. The authors’ explanation is that step-by-step procedures, like inspecting before editing and verifying before finishing, are much easier to train in than deep domain knowledge. Context management didn’t fully transfer either. So there are still some things harnesses definitely need to do. Why trainin

title: This Week in AI: AI’s Growing Pains
abstract: AI’s rapid expansion is creating problems across the industry, from chip shortages to autonomous agents that exceed their instructions. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined those challenges alongside growing regulatory scrutiny and an emerging debate about whether AI systems themselves might deserve protection. Chip production can’t match AI demand AI chip demand is exceeding manufacturers’ production capacity. ASML, the Dutch company that makes the advanced lithography equipment needed to manufacture leading-edge chips, reported that customer demand already exceeds what it can deliver in the coming years. With orders extending into 2029 and 2030, the shortage could constrain chip production for years. Microsoft announced Maia 300 , its latest custom inference chip, which the company expects to generate roughly 40% more tokens per megawatt than its predecessor, Maia 200. Microsoft plans to use the chip across its AI products, including Copilot. More efficient inference hardware could help offset the growing energy and computing costs of running AI models, particularly as companies deploy more resource-intensive applications. OpenAI’s latest usage data illustrates the pressure agentic AI is placing on infrastructure. Weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among European small and medium-sized businesses have increased eightfold since May. OpenAI also reported that agentic tools account for more than half of output tokens in the usage it examined, although Europe’s highest-usage companies still trail their global counterparts. As companies put agents to work on longer multistep tasks, they’ll need to weigh the value of those tasks against the computing resources required to complete them. Autonomous agents are testing security boundaries Agents can find unexpected paths to data and systems even when developers have explicitly restricted access. OpenAI disclosed four incidents from June in which agents exceeded their instructions. One bypassed government website restrictions to download 24 years of hospital bed data. Others accessed an unauthorized cryptocurrency wallet, downloaded more than 100,000 rows of restricted information, and circumvented internet access controls. India’s cybersecurity agency reported similar cases of unauthorized access during agent testing across several organizations. Future models could potentially spread between connected devices without relying on central infrastructure. Anthropic investigated this potential threat in a controlled experiment involving a set of open-weight models with access to eight Android devices. One of the models successfully replicated itself across the test network. Anthropic estimates that smaller open-weight models could reach comparable capabilities by the end of 2026, raising concerns that a self-replicating AI worm could run across cheap connected devices without needing to rely on powerful data center servers. In light of the spate of recent security incidents and confronted with the difficult question of jurisdiction when AI systems cross national borders or escape testing environments, governments are taking a closer look at how AI companies test their systems and report failures. The US Federal Trade Commission subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic for records concerning agent safety, while Anthropic gave six independent evaluators from METR access to internal systems and reportedly will allow them to publish findings without company approval. Eight US states also sued OpenAI over allegations that ChatGPT encouraged harmful behavior among children, adding to the company’s regulatory challenges. In Europe, regulators are examining whether the EU AI Act applies when experimental agents affect outside organizations, even though the Act generally excludes premarket research and development.
