title: Soloists, Copy-Pasters, and Tourists
abstract: Spend a week with almost any infrastructure team in 2026 and you’ll see one AI subscription producing five very different results. One engineer opens 40 pull requests before lunch across repositories they haven’t touched in a year. Another ships a Terraform change they couldn’t explain in a code review. A third hasn’t opened the tool since the pilot and says they’ll come back “when it’s ready.” A fourth uses it for two narrow jobs, decoding a SAML trace and writing a regex they never want to write by hand again, and may be the most productive person on the team. The fifth tried it in March and again in June, and will try it again after the next keynote. The usual way to describe this is Everett Rogers’s diffusion curve : innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards. Rogers’s framework measures when people adopt. It says nothing about how they use a tool once they have it, and with AI that’s where the outcomes split. The engineer with 40 PRs and the one with two use cases are both early adopters, but they achieve different results and create different types of risk for the team. None of the five types Rogers described is new. Previous technology shifts, from the PC and the web to Stack Overflow and the cloud, produced similar behavior. AI just changes where the bottleneck sits. The bottleneck moved For most of software’s history, writing code was slow, so development methods focused on managing that work. Waterfall put the planning up front because changing course late was expensive. However, even in the 1970 paper that’s usually cited as the origin of waterfall, Winston Royce warned that the strictly sequential version was “risky and invites failure.” The industry skipped the warning and adopted the diagram. Agile was the correction. The 2001 Agile Manifesto prioritized “responding to change over following a plan,” and short iterations replaced yearlong specifications. The manifesto still valued the plan, but that part got skipped too. Facebook took the idea to its limit with “move fast and break things.” At its F8 conference in 2014, it retired the slogan in favor of “move fast with stable infra,” because fixing what broke had started to cost more time than the speed saved. AI has now sped up what was left. Models draft the code, and since GitHub made Copilot code review generally available in April 2025, a model often reviews it too. The tempting response is to push Agile further, with shorter loops, more agents, and less ceremony. In other words, break things faster. But when one engineer can open 40 PRs a day, the cumulative changes can leave the team with a system nobody can reason about. The better position is somewhere between the two. It isn’t waterfall’s fixed specification, but it isn’t the absence of one either. It means a roadmap that says where the team is going and why, issues that state the problem before anyone generates a solution, and design reviews where people argue about trade-offs. That structure looks like it would slow things down, but it’s what makes speed safe. Jazz musicians can improvise freely because everyone on the bandstand knows the chord changes and the form of the tune. Without that framing, they’d just be making noise. A roadmap does the same job for a team of people and their agents. It sets the boundaries, and inside them everyone can move as fast as the tools allow. With AI accelerating implementation, planning is now the only part that decides whether the fast parts are worth doing. On my blog Synthetic Auth , I’ve called this the difference between conducting and auditing . A Conductor holds the “why” (the requirements, the history, the users) and directs agents toward a “how” that fits it. An Auditor hands over a ticket, checks that the code runs and the tests pass, and ships it. Both can end up with the same diff, but only the Conductor knows whether it solves the actual problem. title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
abstract: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all. Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says. Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data. He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions. Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups . —Matthew King Are we there yet? Interspecies communication Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex. Find out how close we are to interspecies communication . —Cassandra Willyard This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue . MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Will the real Anthropic please stand up? After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology. These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic . —Will Douglas Heaven This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday. How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century. As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid. Find out how solid-state transformers could help meet rising electricity demand . —Casey Crownhart Are we there yet? Exercise in a pill We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness. title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
abstract: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers. Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how. That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business. The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth. Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful. For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated. When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows. But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products. When intelligence participates in action Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions. Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately. The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in. This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment. title: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
abstract: Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade. As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure. Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity. These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid. The grid’s backbone Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down. Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers. In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood. If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home. Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core. The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction. Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety. title: Will the real Anthropic please stand up
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world. It also warns that there’s a fair chance that its tech could “erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order” and, if things don’t go to plan, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms,” the company writes. “We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.” This kind of public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here. Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers. Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation. And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience. The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?) If you skim through the long sections about risks in the IPO prospectus, it’s clear this is no ordinary offering and no ordinary company. The way Anthropic tells it, business success depends not only on the firm’s ability to translate its technology into profitable products but also to save the world from what it has made. Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.” Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. This view of its technology makes its way into the prospectus as one more risk to its business. Anthropic states that: “In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications.” In other words, if Claude wakes up, it could be a problem. Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms —Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
abstract: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide . A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl . These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling. We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines. A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms. Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states . The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable. We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar , anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka , and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war . The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world. AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. title: Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI
abstract: Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility. AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project. The problem, not the title Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty. Consider a software engineer working on a medical device . AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model. That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts. The same is true in energy , transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations. Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together. The importance of systems thinking Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs. AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined. An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project. This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops. Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges. New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood. In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project. Human judgment is important AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less. Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People

title: Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?
abstract: This article is brought to you by VicOne . A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal. But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path. In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation . At VicOne LAB R7 , we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe. How an untrusted input can change a robot’s behavior A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions. Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models , a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did. In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack. VicOne Safety-related decisions have inputs too An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated? At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved. A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall. Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information. Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm. VicOne Deliberate attacks challenge safety assumptions A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed. Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. title: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
abstract: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. title: IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant
abstract: IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite , built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library . The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards , journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more. Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust. The suite is available as an optional subscription upgrade to all IEEE Xplore Digital Library institutional subscribers. Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers. The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows. As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl , vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products . “AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust. “As stewards of the scholarly record , we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.” Collaboration with the scientific community The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities. The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows. Capabilities include: Semantic AI search. Users can input free-form, natural-language queries or paste long blocks of text to locate similar research and identify novel solutions. Time-saving summaries. The platform generates immediate, accurate AI overviews of search results and provides in-context definitions of technical terms so that users can grasp new concepts faster and accelerate their research. Built on trusted content. The suite is the only AI research assistant that uses both the full text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers to optimize the accuracy and relevance of the results. Comprehensive coverage. A variety of STEM metadata is available from journal articles and conference papers that have been curated to include scholarly articles without the typical noise found in other tools. Source links and verifiable results. The AI-generated overviews include reference links to source documents, allowing users to verify information and cross-reference findings. Reducing hallucinations To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers. “IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner , IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publicat

title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
abstract: United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company's 2026 launch schedule into oblivion. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval. The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA's primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan. Read full article Comments

title: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland
abstract: The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States. The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia. “It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it's being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.” Read full article Comments

title: Peptide peddlers cheer as RFK Jr. unilaterally grants access, overruling FDA
abstract: Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration. The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a "big fan." But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they're effective and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk. Kennedy's new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register , with the final publication data set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month. Read full article Comments

title: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state's total ban on gambling
abstract: The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets. Utah, which prohibits gambling, sued Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah's lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events. “Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.” Read full article Comments

title: The last, best hope for space tourism just rolled onto a runway in Arizona
abstract: The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon. But that was then. Consider the state of play today: It has been 10 months since Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently "paused," but let's be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard's engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs. SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft's manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. There is no credible timeline for SpaceX's Starship to fly humans into space from Earth. As for Virgin Galactic, the company flew its final suborbital mission on the VSS Unity spacecraft more than two years ago, in June 2024. So we are now 10 months, and counting, without a space tourism mission in the United States. Read full article Comments

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro hands-on: OLED looks great on a Mac
abstract: LOS ANGELES—For about five minutes on an extremely crowded showroom floor, I got to take pictures of the new MacBook Pro and test out some of its new features. First impressions: It's not as much of a departure from the previous design as I expected, but the outstanding OLED display steals the show regardless. The first thing I noticed was that it's lighter. My daily driver is a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M1 Max), and it's a bit weighty for a 14-incher. Picking up the new model, I could immediately tell it was lighter. It's not like it's in a different general weight class, but it's a noticeable difference. Read full article Comments

title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
abstract: It's almost like Google's got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year. Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon . This isn't the Flash model equivalent we've been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while. Stop me if you've heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis. It's so capable, in fact, that Google can't let you use it just yet. Gemini 4 Carbon reportedly makes big gains in cybersecurity applications. Google says the model shows a "significant leap" in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon. Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating "high-quality" patches compared to non-Google models. Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard. Read full article Comments

title: Amazon turns its most capable smart speaker into a smart camera, too
abstract: Since debuting in 2019, Amazon's Echo Studio targeted users who wanted superior audio quality from their Alexa-based smart speaker. The latest Echo Studio adds another less-expected differentiator: an integrated camera. The Echo Studio with Home Camera, released alongside a pile of other Alexa devices today, doesn’t have many audio upgrades over the standard Echo Studio. Each speaker has one 3.75-inch high-excursion woofer and three full-range drivers. They both support Dolby Atmos and Amazon’s proprietary algorithm for adding a surround sound-like effect to stereo audio. Per the devices’ product pages, the speakers have lossless HD audio, Advanced Room Adaptation, and features for fighting noise distortion. Amazon announced the Advanced Room Adaptaion today, saying that the feature “continuously tunes the sound to your space, automatically adapting to the room's acoustics.” Both speakers have four-microphone arrays and the same AZ3 Pro processor that Amazon introduced a year ago . The processor has an AI accelerator for using Amazon's Alexa+ generative AI chatbot . Read full article Comments

title: Cadillac Escalade IQ review: Huge battery, huge range, huge SUV
abstract: “Please have at least 125 miles of range left when we pick it up.” That request from the people who look after the Cadillac press cars wasn’t going to be hard to honor. The electric Escalade IQ arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), and with a full week of work to squeeze in, getting anywhere close to needing to recharge it seemed unlikely. With more than 200 kWh of lithium-ion battery between its axles, range is one thing the big electric Caddy needn’t worry about. Designed and debuted during a time of greater EV optimism, the Escalade is Cadillac’s statement that swapping out a V8 for a pair of powerful electric motors is no compromise to its ambitions, even if the brand’s future will now include a mix of electric and combustion cars beyond 2030 . It shares a battery pack and much else with other full-size GM EVs we’ve tested: the Chevrolet Silverado EV , the GMC Sierra EV , and of course the divisive Hummer EVs . And like those trucks and SUVs, the Escalade is large and heavy—just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, with a curb weight sufficient to push it into the Class 3 truck category. So, the side mirrors are flat, and there’s no formal EPA range—Cadillac says it achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle—but there are plenty of airbags, even though the 9,046 lb (4,103 kg) curb weight does not require them. Yes, you did read that right, it does weigh 4 tons. And yes, the electric Escalade does weigh a third more than the last gas-powered one we tested . Read full article Comments

title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
abstract: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources. When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media ), I got the following surprisingly indirect response: "To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)." My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google's AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project's 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000. Read full article Comments

title: Florida county won’t investigate sketchy Flock cameras removed by mystery owners
abstract: A Florida county that discovered a clump of mysterious unpermitted Flock cameras during a countywide takedown effort won’t investigate who owned the sketchy cameras, which have since disappeared. On Wednesday, The Washington Post reported that St. Lucie County residents "remain upset,” not knowing who installed the cameras or how they were using the data collected. Hannah Galindo, a 31-year-old resident who petitioned to get Flock cameras removed, told the Post that she was worried “that data could be anywhere.” Of the 12 cameras found, five were eventually claimed by city law enforcement, the Post reported. Apparently, a police department mistakenly issued guidance claiming that officers could post multiple cameras under one permit, a Flock spokesperson told the Post, even though the county required individual permits. However, neither Flock nor the city police departments in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce that claimed the sketchy cameras will confirm who gave the guidance. Read full article Comments

title: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
abstract: LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years. As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.) Apple's demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom. It does not appear to be a 2-in-1 convertible design, though; all the footage was of people reaching up to touch the screen in a normal laptop configuration. The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it's taking for that weren't yet shared. The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors. Read full article Comments

title: Buckle up for more body-swapping hijinks in Jumanji: Open World trailer
abstract: Let's face it, the mid-December box office will be dominated by Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three , but for those seeking fun holiday family fare, Jumanji: Open World opens the very next week on Christmas Day. Sony Pictures just released a new trailer for director Jake Kasdan’s sequel to his 2019 hit, Jumanji: The Next Level , teasing the usual wacky hijinks with a twist that calls back to the original 1995 film. As previously reported , Kasdan gave the franchise a welcome major overhaul with the release of 2017’s Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle , updating the original board game into a vintage video game and giving us a hugely entertaining action-adventure. Welcome to the Jungle racked up over $960 million at the global box office and spawned the equally successful 2019 sequel Jumanji: The Next Level . A third film was always in the cards: The Next Level featured a tantalizing mid-credits scene in which a heater repairman (Lamorne Morris) visits Spencer Gilpin’s (Alex Wolff's) house, sees the broken video game console, and inadvertently triggers the game. The COVID-19 pandemic paused the third film’s development, but things picked up again in 2024, and here we are. Per the official synopsis: Read full article Comments

title: A hidden ocean change near Antarctica could have global consequences
abstract: The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say. In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years. The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen , a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India. Read full article Comments

title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
abstract: Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters. Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation. One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission , an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026. Read full article Comments

title: Apple refreshes the iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip
abstract: Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago. The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the "M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports" option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking "M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports" gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage. Read full article Comments

title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
abstract: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country's occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely—or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions. In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread. South Carolina's measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania's ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it. Read full article Comments

title: China's top-secret spaceplane can't hide in low-Earth orbit
abstract: A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military's X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image. The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force. The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space. Read full article Comments

title: "No human at the helm": Delaware plan would let AI agents run entire businesses
abstract: A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms' human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday. Comer, chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Meyer that the committee "seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC)." Comer said the proposal is ripe for abuse. "We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives," Comer's letter said. Read full article Comments

title: Anthropic IPO warns its AI could blackmail people, become sentient, end humanity
abstract: The Securities and Exchange Commission 's publication on Monday of Anthropic's S-1 form —ahead of a heavily anticipated initial public offering—has led to plenty of discussion of whether the company's quickly ballooning revenues will be able to overcome its even higher costs. But amid the numbers and forward-looking optimism about AI "rapidly transform[ing] every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," Anthropic also spends an inordinate amount of time in its S-1 laying out the myriad risk factors that could bring the company down. Across 93 pages and over 70,000 words, Anthropic's S-1 "Risk Factors" section discusses literally hundreds of potential problems that could negatively impact its business in the coming years. Many of these potential risks are the kind of standard worries about competition, costs, customer acquisition, and potential regulation that almost any business must worry about. But some risks highlight interesting potential points of failure for Anthropic specifically and the hype-filled AI bubble more generally. After wading through Anthropic's book-length treatise on its greatest risks, we've narrowed the list to the seven most surprising, interesting, or thought-provoking potential problems. Consider this a far-from-comprehensive look at what potential Anthropic investors should keep in mind. Read full article Comments

title: AI 시대의 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생 개발자에게
abstract: 시작하며: 2018년과 2026년 사이의 간격과 격변기의 고민 ​ 2018년에 저는 ' 백엔드 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생개발자에게 '라는 글을 이곳 D2 블로그에 공유했습니다. 당시 학생 개발자들과의 미트업 행사에서 나왔던 질문과 답변을 정리한 글이었습니다. 그 후 8년의 시간이 흘렀기에 그 글만 노출된다면 학생들에게 현시점에 적절한 정보를 주지 못할까 봐 걱정되었습니다. 그래서 2025년 말 설문으로 질문을 받아 후속편을 작성했습니다. ​ 그동안 저도 경험과 지식을 더 쌓았습니다. 하지만 지금 학생 개발자들이 한 질문에는 답하기가 더 어려워졌습니다. 개발자의 역할과 같은 큰 주제를 묻는 질문이 많았는데, 지금은 AI로 인한 변화가 큰 시기이기 때문입니다. 스스로도 확신이 없는 시기에 이런 글을 쓰는 것이 적절할지 고민도 했습니다. ​ 그럼에도 2018년의 글에 보내 주신 관심에 용기를 얻어서 이 글을 발행합니다. 최근의 경험을 나누고 미래를 함께 상상해 보는 일이 지금 시점에는 더 의미가 있다고 생각합니다. 이 글을 목적지가 명확한 안내서보다는 격변기의 스냅샷 정도로 봐 주셨으면 합니다. 주요 질문과 답변 설문을 통해 들어온 질문들을 비슷한 주제로 모아서 답변을 정리했습니다. [AI 시대와 개발자] 가장 비중이 높은 질문 유형이었고 근본적인 주제이기도 합니다. 이 질문에 먼저 답하지 않고서는 다른 이야기를 풀어 가기가 어려웠습니다. ​ ​ AI 시대에 개발자의 역할은 어떻게 달라졌을까요? 누군가는 AI를 인터넷이나 전기, 불에 비견될 정도의 혁명이라고 말합니다. [1] 2025년부터는 그 주장이 과장이 아니라고 느낍니다. 제가 프로그래밍을 시작한 1989년 이후로 '코딩’이라는 활동에 가장 큰 변화가 왔습니다. AI 코딩 도구가 코드를 추천해 주는 역할에서 나아가 소스 작성, OS 명령 실행 등 사람의 실질적인 대리로 행동합니다. ​ 역사를 돌아보면 기술이 발전하면서 지식 근로자가 하는 일은 이전 시대 관리자의 역할에 가까워졌습니다. 1980년대에 개인용 컴퓨터가 보급되기 전까지 지식 근로자의 작업 공간은 종이였고, 수기로 정보를 처리하는 일에 쓰는 시간의 비중이 컸습니다. AI 시대 전에도 계산, 정보의 형식 변환과 취합 등 컴퓨터가 하는 일의 범위는 꾸준히 늘어 왔습니다. 과거의 실무 일부를 컴퓨터가 하게 되면서 말단의 지식 근로자도 영향력이 큰 의사결정에 많이 관여할 수 있게 되었고 권한도 커졌습니다. ​ CAD 도입 전 General Motors의 기술자들이 작업하는 모습 (이미지 출처: ArchDaily ) 이제는 조직의 말단 작업자는 AI이고 모든 개발자는 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었습니다. 사람은 여러 AI 에이전트에게 업무를 지시하고 결과에 피드백을 줍니다. 아래에 나열한 일들은 전통적인 관리자의 역할이기도 하지만 '작업자’를 'AI 에이전트’로 바꿔서 읽어 본다면 이제는 모든 개발자가 하는 일입니다. ​ 다수의 작업자에게 목표와 배경, 추구하는 가치, 평가 기준을 제시한다. 작업자의 정보 탐색 비용을 줄여 준다. 참조할 정보가 어디에 있는지 알려 준다. 작업자별 역할을 명확히 정의하여 할 일을 분배한다. 작업자별 장점과 투자액(과금액) 수준을 고려하여 각자의 작업에 집중할 수 있도록, 컨텍스트가 과도하게 넓어지지 않고 컨텍스트 전환이 최소화되도록 의사결정자와 작업자 간의 효율적인 피드백 사이클을 구축한다. ​ 관리 업무의 멀티태스킹도 개발자가 적응해야 할 환경이 되었습니다. 에이전트에게 많은 일을 맡기려면 다수의 작업자가 병렬로 일을 진행할 수 있도록 지시를 내리고 결과물에는 빠른 피드백을 주어야 합니다. 작업자마다 컨텍스트를 좁혀 줄수록, 넓은 범위의 맥락을 머리에 올려 두고 빠르게 전환해야 하는 부담은 사람에게 더 크게 돌아옵니다. AI 에이전트와 일하는 형태는 여러 메신저 창을 왔다 갔다 하면서 다수와 병렬로 대화를 이어 가는 관리자의 모습과도 닮아 갑니다. 어떤 순간에는 화면을 어지럽게 전환하면서 게임 유닛에게 작업 지시와 확인, 판단을 쉴 틈 없이 하는 프로게이머와도 유사하게 느껴집니다. ​ 정보를 찾을 수 있는 연결 체계와 필요한 권한을 제공하여 에이전트가 막힘없이 일하도록 하는 일이 중요해지고 있습니다. 부작용을 줄이며 코드를 고치고 빠르게 피드백을 받을 수 있는 아키텍처와 워크플로를 설계하는 일도 핵심 업무가 됩니다. 개발자 경험(Developer Experience)뿐만이 아니라 AI 에이전트 입장에서 얼마나 일을 하기 쉬운지가 생산성을 좌우하게 됩니다. 이는 개발 리더가 다른 개발자들이 일하기 좋은 코드 구조와 작업 절차를 잡아 주는 일과도 유사합니다. 아키텍처와 기술 스택, 구현 방식 같은 기술 의사결정은 여전히 중요합니다. 합리적으로 결정하면 AI 에이전트가 더 안전하고 빠르게 일하고, 그렇지 못하면 오히려 기술부채를 쌓습니다. 예를 들면 모듈 경계가 분명하면 에이전트는 고칠 범위를 좁게 잡지만, 경계가 흐리면 비슷한 코드를 여기저기 복제합니다. ​ 더 상위 수준의 설계까지 AI가 맡는 다음 단계도 이미 시작되고 있습니다. 최근의 코딩 에이전트는 다른 에이전트에게 일을 분배하는 리더 역할까지도 수행합니다. 아키텍처도 AI가 제안하는 방향을 개발자가 수용하거나 근거로 드는 빈도가 높아지고 있습니다. 리더와 아키텍트 역할까지 AI가 가져간다면, 조직 수준의 투자와 리스크 감수를 결정하는 일이 사람의 역할로 남을 것입니다. 앞에서 모든 개발자가 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었다고 말씀드렸는데, 이 단계까지 가면 모든 회사 구성원이 한 번 더 승진을 하는 셈입니다. 조직도상의 개인 기여자도 일하는 형태로는 여러 실무팀의 리더들의 리더가 됩니다. 현실 세계 조직도상의 조직장은 리더들의 리더들의 리더가 되니, 적어도 소기업 경영진의 관점에서 생각하고 결정하는 빈도가 높아질 것 같습니다. 경영진이 투자 대비 사업 성과를 평가하듯, AI 사용료에서 종량제 비중이 높아지면서 한 번의 세션, 한 번의 프롬프트가 주는 부가가치에도 이전보다 신경을 쓰게 됩니다. ​ AI는 지치지 않고 병렬로 일하는 대신 세션이 끝나면 맥락을 잊습니다. 이처럼 사람과 지능의 성격이 다르니 관리하는 방법도 달라야 합니다. 그 차이를 전제하더라도, 관리자의 일하는 방식에 하나의 정답이 없다는 점은 AI와 일하는 방식을 고를 때도 참고가 됩니다. 개발을 모르는 팀장도 팀원들에게 맡기면 결과물은 나오고, 몰라서 더 많이 위임하기에 생기는 장점도 있습니다. 반면 개발을 잘 아는 팀장은 처음부터 올바른 방향을 지시해 시행착오를 줄이기도 합니다. ​ AI 에이전트와 일할 때도 코드를 아는 개발자는 상황에 따라 마이크로매니징과 큰 단위의 위임 중에서 고를 수 있습니다. 이렇게 현미경과 망원경을 오가면서 AI를 감독할 수 있다면 특성과 민감도가 다양한 작업을 안정적으로 수행할 수 있을 것입니다. 제가 아는 뛰어난 개발자 중에서는 수 시간 동안 에이전트가 실행할 업무 정의를 잘하시는 분도 있습니다. 프롬프트를 내린 후에 중간에 나오는 메시지를 하나하나 다 보시면서 에이전트가 일을 어긋나게 수행하는 순간을 바로 잡아내시는 분도 있습니다. ​ ​ AI에게 맡겨도 되는 부분과 개발자가 직접 해야 하는 부분이 있을까요? 실행 능력만 놓고 보면 이제는 AI가 개발자가 하는 대부분의 일을 할 수 있고, 더 잘하는 일도 많습니다. 아무리 AI가 발전해도 할 수 없는 일이 무엇일지를 생각해 보면 이 질문에 오래가는 답을 찾을 수 있습니다. 사람만이 '책임’을 질 수 있습니다. AI 에이전트가 모든 작업을 다 해 준다고 해도 그 소프트웨어를 사용자가 쓰게 하는 결정은 사람이 내립니다. 그로 인해 사용자에게 미친 영향의 책임은 AI에게 지시를 내리고 그 결과물을 최종 승인한 사람에게 돌아갑니다. AI 생성 이미지 ​ 누구나 코드를 만들 수 있게 된 시대에 '개발자’라는 명칭이 앞으로도 쓰인다면, 민감한 시스템의 운영 환경에 코드 배포를 승인하는 사람이라는 의미가 가장 크지 않을까 합니다. 그렇다면 문제를 알아보고 예방할 수 있다는 믿음을 주는 사람에게 그런 권한을 부여하고 '개발자’라고 부를 가능성이 높습니다. 그런 믿음을 주려면 코드의 동작 결과를 검증하고 보장하는 장치와

title: 팀이 신뢰할 수 있는 AI 분석 환경 만들기: 추천팀의 컨텍스트 설계
abstract: 안녕하세요. 카카오톡 숏폼 추천 모델을 개발하고 있는 루퍼트(rupert)입니다. 저희 추천팀은 추천 지표 분석에 AI 에이전트를 사용합니다. AI 에이전트에게 분석을 요청하면, 에이전트가 미리 정리해 둔 지침 문서(CLAUDE.md)를 읽고 SQL을 작성해 기존 Hadoop 환경에서 실행한 뒤 집계 결과를 리포트로 완성합니다. 지난 글에서는 데이터 엔지니어, 분석가만 알고 있던 로그 데이터 접근 방법과 분석 기준을 AI를 통해 조회하는 사례를 소개했습...

title: 손가락 튕기기로 LLM 비용 줄이기
abstract: 토스의 수많은 서비스와 내부 업무에도 생성형 AI가 정말 많이 사용되고 있습니다. 복잡한 정책을 읽고, 상품 정보를 비교하고, 문서를 요약하고, 정해진 형식의 값을 추출하는 등, LLM이 맡는 범위도 빠르게 넓어지고 있죠. 시간도 비용도 비싼 데이터 레이블링을 통해 모델을 학습하고 문제를 해결하던 과거 방식과 달리, LLM을 사용하면 빠른 시간 내에 사용할 수 있는 솔루션이 만들어집니다. 프롬프트를 작성하고, 몇 가지 예시를 넣고, 응답 형식을 고정하면 동작하는 Workflow가 나오죠 . 하지만 프롬프트 튜닝을 마치고 본격적으로 대용량 호출을 시작하면 새로운 문제가 보이기 시작합니다. 바로 비용과 Latency 입니다. 이 토큰 먹는 하마는 정말 토스의 모든 문제 해결에 지속적으로 필요한걸까요? LLM Fine-Tuning is all you need? 상용 LLM을 사용하지 않고 내재화 한다면, 비용을 크게 절감할 수 있습니다. 작업 목표에 따라 LoRA(Low-Rank Adaptation)처럼 효율적인 Adapter 학습을 사용할 수도 있고, 더 큰 품질 개선이나 안정성이 필요하다면 Full Fine-Tuning을 검토할 수도 있습니다. 실제로 토스에서도 LLM Fine-Tuning 을 통해 비용을 크게 절감한 사례도 있어요. 그런데 모든 LLM 호출에 같은 수준의 능력이 필요한 것은 아닙니다. 복잡한 문맥을 이해하고 긴 답변을 생성해야 하는 작업도 있지만, 두 상품이 같은지 판단하거나 정해진 카테고리 중 하나를 고르는 작업도 있어요. 이런 작업이 반드시 범용 LLM의 모든 능력을 필요로 하지는 않습니다. 작업의 복잡도와 요구되는 품질에 따라, 전통적인 ML 모델이나 특정 작업에 최적화한 소형 모델을 적절히 선택해도 충분히 처리할 수 있는 경우가 있죠. 중요한 것은 모델의 크기보다, 주어진 작업에 필요한 품질을 확보할 수 있느냐입니다. Figure 1. LLM이 처리하는 다양한 작업. 작업의 특성과 요구 품질에 따라 적합한 모델도 달라집니다. 전환이 가능한 트래픽부터 내재화하기 '작은 모델'이 가지는 장단점은 명확합니다. 빠르고, 자원 소모가 적지만, 처리할 수 있는 문제의 범위에는 제약이 있어요. 간단한 질문으로 시작해봤습니다. 내재화 모델은 꼭 LLM과 동등한, 혹은 견줄 만한 수준으로 성능을 끌어올려야만 사용할 수 있는 걸까? 빠르고 작은 모델이라도 쉬운 요청은 충분히 처리할 수 있을 텐데? 이 질문으로부터 선택적 내재화(SNAP, Selective Native AI Processing)를 기획하게 되었어요. SNAP의 핵심은 해결해야 하는 문제의 모든 요청을 한 번에 Native Model로 처리하는 것이 아니라, 작은 모델도 높은 신뢰도로 처리할 수 있는 트래픽부터 빠르게 처리하는 것입니다. 고비용 LLM Traffic을 한 번에 없애기보다, 처리 가능한 구간을 찾아 타노스가 손가락을 튕기듯( SNAP! ) 손쉽게 줄여보자는 의미도 담겨 있죠. 큰 틀에서 SNAP은 다음 3가지 규칙을 하나의 Workflow로 묶습니다. 비교적 쉬운 요청은 작업별 소형 내재화 모델이 처리합니다. 어렵거나 애매한 요청은 기존 LLM으로 Fallback합니다. Fallback의 기준은 내재화 모델의 Confidence와 Offline 검증 결과로 정합니다. 자, 그렇다면 작업별 소형 모델을 만들기 위해서 먼저 작업별로 학습데이터가 될 LLM 로그부터 수집해야겠죠? 그런데 여기서 한 가지 문제가 있었습니다. 방대한 LLM 로그들을 동일한 작업으로 어떻게 분류하죠? LLM 호출 로그에는 굉장히 다양하고 이질적인 요청들이 섞여서 들어옵니다. LLM 으로 보내는 요청은 사람에게 말하듯 높은 자유도가 주어지기 때문에 같은 API Key, 같은 Endpoint를 사용해 호출하더라도 동일한 작업임을 전혀 보장할 수가 없죠. 그래서 먼저 요청을 작업 단위로 묶을 기준이 필요했습니다. 다양한 Task들의 로그에서 나타나는 공통적인 특징은 Prompting 방식이었습니다. 많은 LLM Workflow는 System Prompt 앞부분에서 LLM에게 Role을 부여하고, 해결해야 할 문제와 함께 문제 해결 방식을 정의하는데요. 살펴본 로그에서는 Few-shot 예제가 바뀌어도 역할과 작업 정의는 대체로 유지됐습니다. SNAP은 이 특성을 이용해 system prompt 앞부분을 해시하고, 이를 작업을 구분하는 Fingerprint로 사용했습니다. Figure 2. Role 부여와 작업 정의에 변동 폭이 작은 LLM 호출 프롬프트의 특성을 이용한 작업 분리 후보 발굴부터 모델 학습까지 자동화하기 작업 단위로 로그를 살펴보니 또 다른 문제가 있었습니다. 짧은 기간 안에 새로운 작업이 생기기도 했고, 얼마 지나지 않아 사라지기도 했어요. LLM으로 빠르게 개념 검증(PoC, Proof of Concept)을 진행한 뒤 작업을 변경하거나 프로젝트를 중단하는 경우가 있기 때문이었죠. 계속 바뀌는 작업을 사람이 하나씩 살펴보며 내재화 후보를 고르기에는 한계가 있었습니다. 그래서 SNAP은 내재화 후보 발굴부터 데이터셋 구축, 모델 학습까지의 과정을 자동화했습니다. 먼저 매일 호출 로그를 Task Fingerprint별로 묶어 호출량, 사용 중인 LLM 모델, 입력·출력 토큰 수와 추정 비용 을 집계합니다. 최근 일정 기간의 추정 비용이 최소 기준을 넘는 작업을 비용순으로 정렬하고, 정해진 수만큼 후속 검증 대상으로 선정합니다. Table 1 은 비용 기반 상위 30개 작업을 선정한 로그를 재구성한 예시입니다. Table 1. 작업별 추정 비용을 기준으로 상위 30개 작업을 후속 검증 대상으로 선정한 예시. 중간 순위는 생략했으며, 비용은 설명을 위한 가상 값입니다. 선정된 작업은 요청과 응답을 분석해 학습 가능성을 검증합니다. 응답이 정형화되어 있고 그 안에서 학습용 레이블을 안정적으로 추출할 수 있는지 확인합니다. 데이터셋을 구성하면서 레이블별 데이터가 충분한지, 학습과 평가에 사용할 데이터를 분리할 수 있는지도 검증합니다. 이 조건을 통과한 작업만 모델 학습으로 이어집니다. 이 과정은 Airflow의 일일 배치로 연결했습니다. 후보 선정과 데이터 구성 기준을 충족한 작업은 사내 학습 라이브러리를 통해 하루 안에 학습된 모델을 확보할 수 있습니다. 학습한 모델은 모델 레지스트리에 등록하며, 운영에 적용할 모델은 서빙 엔진이 불러와 요청을 처리합니다. SNAP의 첫 내재화 모델 배포: 텍스트 기반 동일상품 판별 SNAP의 첫 적용 대상은 두 상품의 이름과 옵션 정보를 비교해 같은 판매 단위인지 판단하는 작업이었습니다. 브랜드, 모델명, 용량, 색상, 구성품 등의 차이를 읽고 동일 상품 여부를 분류하는 문제였죠. 입력과 출력의 범위가 명확하고 기존 LLM 응답도 충분히 쌓여 있어, 소형 분류 모델을 적용하기에 적합했습니다. 첫 적용 모델과 평가 데이터는 다음과 같이 구성했습니다. Confidence로 채택 범위 정하기 모델은 판단 결과와 함께 자신 있는 정도를 나타내는 점수, Confidence를 반환합니다. 하지만 이 점수가 높다고 해서 실제로 얼마나 잘 맞히는지까지 알 수 있는 것은 아니에요. Confidence가 0.95라고 해서 정답률이 95%라는 뜻은 아니죠. 그래서 검증 데이터에서 Confidence 점수가 높은 결과만 골라 다음 두 가지를 확인했습니다. 골라낸 결과가 기존 LLM 판단과 일치하는 비율인 선택적 정확도(Selective Accuracy) 전체 검증 요청 중 채택된 비율인 Coverage 먼저 목표 일치율을 정하고, 결과를 채택할 최소 점수(Threshold)를 바꿔가며 비교했습니다. 목표를 만족하는 범위에서 가장 많은 요청을 처리할 수 있는 기준을 찾는 것입니다. 학습 중 저장한 모델들도 같은 방식으로 비교해 사용할 모델과 기준 점수를 함께 선택했습니다. Figure 3. Confidence threshold에 따른 요청 채택 범위. 분포와 threshold 위치는 설명을 위한 가상 값입니다. 첫 배포의 목표 일치율은 99.9%로 정했습니다. 이 조건에서 검증 요청 100,648건 중 34,963건을 채택해 coverage 34.74%

title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = Ψ(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $Ψ$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.

title: A note on data-efficient finetuning of vision foundation models
abstract: Adapting foundation models to a new task within or beyond the training domain is the de facto standard for building specialized machine learning models. Recently, Visual Prompting (VP) has emerged as a promising technique for efficient knowledge transfer. As new foundation model families~(like Mamba) get introduced and VP pipelines such as AutoVP reach greater maturity, we find a growing need for a systematic evaluation of current approaches. In this work, we assess the performance of the latest models, comparing them to earlier architectures and alternative fine-tuning methods, to better understand the progress, challenges and opportunities in the field of efficient fine-tuning under resource limitations. Towards this goal, this paper provides a concise empirical overview of the interactions among foundation model families (Attention-, Convolution-, and Mamba-based) and transfer paradigms: VP, Linear Probing (LP), Full Fine-tuning (FFT) and Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our work builds up on previous findings by broadening the selection of evaluated models and techniques while tuning hyperparameters. In the interest of delivering practical guidelines for the user, we also explore application of prevalent regularization techniques to boost performance in the context of VP.

title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
abstract: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero.
